question: Does this change to a product make users do better?

kohavi2020.cite: Kohavi et al. (2020). Online randomized controlled experiments at scale: lessons and extensions to medicine. Trials 21: 150.
kohavi2020.checked: every quote read word for word in the Europe PMC full text (PMC7007661) on 20 Nov 2026; places are given as sections; in-text reference numbers are left out of the quotes

steps.title: Build variants
steps.text: Make the change (B) and keep the current version (A). Only that one thing differs.

quotes.text: Every major technology company runs online controlled experiments, often called A/B tests, to gather trustworthy data and make data-driven decisions about how to improve their products. All these controlled experiments are randomized.

steps.title: Agree the metric
steps.text: Before the test, agree on the one measure (or few) that decides success. Hundreds of other metrics are for understanding, not for picking a winner.

quotes.text: Agreement on the Overall Evaluation Criterion (OEC) becomes critically important.
Since the OEC is used to determine success (e.g., shipping a change) and consists of one or a few metrics, there is less concern about multiple hypothesis testing.

steps.title: Split at random
steps.text: Each user is assigned to A or B by chance as they arrive. Huge numbers make tiny effects detectable.

quotes.text: For Bing, Google, and LinkedIn, it is common for each experiment to be exposed to over a million users.
the ability to detect an effect twice as small, e.g., 0.25%, requires quadrupling the number of users.

steps.title: Check the split
steps.text: Before reading results, check that the arms got the share of users they should. A lopsided split means something broke.

quotes.text: If the experiment design is for a ratio of one-to-one (equally sized control and treatment) then deviations in the actual ratio of users in an experiment likely indicate a problem.
quotes.where: Similarities and dissimilarities with medical RCTs

steps.title: Ship or drop
steps.text: Ship the winner, change or drop the loser, and test the next idea. Most ideas turn out not to help.

quotes.text: Winners are shipped, losers are modified (given new data and insights from the experiment) or abandoned.
most ideas are not as good as we believe

forking-paths.text: It is usually easy to find something that improves (or degrades), but the challenge is to come up with a small set of key metrics, ideally a single OEC, to help make tradeoffs.

construct-validity.text: A good OEC captures the organizational long-term objectives but must be based on metrics that are measurable in short-term experiments.

exercise.title: A/A tests: when nothing changed
exercise.intro: In an A/A test both arms see exactly the same product, so any difference is chance. Run a batch of 100 and count the 'significant' ones; then let each test look at more metrics.

quote.text: Because the null hypothesis is true by design in A/A tests, statistically significant differences for each metric should happen at about 5% when using a p value cutoff of 0.05.
quote.where: Similarities and dissimilarities with medical RCTs

exercise.data_label: Example data, simulated for this exercise.
exercise.model: Each arm has 1000 users who convert at 5%; a metric counts as significant when a two-sided z-test gives p < 0.05. Metrics are simulated as independent, which real metrics are not.
